title: Stargazing: the Moon, bright stars and planets, and why the Moon seems to follow you

summary.text: Ride in a bus at night, and the Moon seems to come along with you. The trees rush past, but the Moon keeps up. In this unit your child walks past a window and finds out why: the Moon is so far away that a few steps hardly change where it is. Your child also learns to tell the Moon, stars, planets and aeroplanes apart. Stars are faraway suns that twinkle, because moving air shakes their light. Planets shine with sunlight, usually without twinkling.
summary.art: A girl at a bus window at night, trees blurring past outside, and a round Moon sitting still above them.

intro.hook: Have you ever looked at the Moon from a moving bus, car or auto? What did the Moon do?
intro.text: Most children say the Moon followed them. The trees and lamp posts rushed past, but the Moon stayed beside the window. Is the Moon really following you? In this unit you test it at your own window. You also find out which bright dots in the night sky are stars, which are planets, and which are aeroplanes.
intro.art: A boy and his mother in an auto at night, the boy pointing up at the Moon, with street lamps streaking past.

outcomes: By the end I can find the Moon and bright stars in the night sky, and tell them from an aeroplane.
By the end I can show that the Moon seems to follow me because it is very far away.
By the end I can say that the Moon and the planets shine with light from the Sun, and that stars make their own light.
By the end I can show, with the hot tawa test, that moving air makes a small light twinkle.
By the end I can say that stars usually twinkle and planets usually shine steadily, and that planets wander slowly among the stars.

terms.meaning: The Moon is a big ball of rock that goes round the Earth. It makes no light of its own. It shines because sunlight falls on it.
terms.example: The Moon takes about a month to go once round the Earth.
terms.art: The Earth with the grey, rocky Moon beside it, and the Sun far off to one side, lighting one half of the Moon.

terms.meaning: A star is a huge ball of very hot gas that makes its own light. The Sun is our nearest star.
terms.example: The stars at night are suns too. They look tiny because they are very, very far away.
terms.art: A big bright Sun on the left, and a dark sky full of tiny star dots on the right.

terms.meaning: A planet is a big ball that goes round the Sun. The Earth is a planet. Other planets shine in our sky with the Sun's light.
terms.example: Venus is a planet. It is the brightest planet in our sky, brighter than any star.
terms.art: A bright steady dot low over the sea after sunset, with an orange glow where the Sun went down.

terms.meaning: A star twinkles when its light seems to flicker and shiver. The moving air above us wobbles its light.
terms.example: Stars low down near the rooftops twinkle the most. Planets usually shine more steadily.
terms.art: A star drawn with little flicker marks around it, above a rooftop, and a steady round dot beside it.

explanations.concept: The Moon seems to follow you because it is very far away
explanations.definition: When you move, near things seem to slide past you, and far things hardly seem to move. The Moon is so far away that it seems to stay in the same place, so it looks as if it comes along with you.
explanations.description: In the window strip test, the paper strips slid past the Moon when you walked. A far building slid a little, and the Moon stayed in the same place. The Moon is about 3,84,000 kilometres away, so a few steps make almost no difference to where you see it.
examples: In the window strip test, the paper strips slid past, and the Moon stayed put.
From a moving train, the poles by the track flash past, far hills move slowly, and the Moon seems to keep up.
In the tumbler test, the near tumbler jumped across the far wall when you took two steps.
explanations.context: This card explains why the Moon seems to follow you.
explanations.art: A child walking past a window with three paper strips on the glass, the strips sliding past while the Moon stays in the same place.

explanations.concept: The Moon and the planets shine with sunlight
explanations.definition: The Moon and the planets make no light of their own. We see them because sunlight falls on them and bounces off into our eyes.
explanations.description: The Moon is a ball of grey rock. At night the Sun is shining on the other side of the Earth, but its light still reaches the Moon and bounces off it to us. Venus, Jupiter, Mars and Saturn shine in the same way.
examples: The bright side of the Moon always faces the Sun.
Venus shines brightly just after sunset, lit by the Sun that has just gone down.
A steel plate in a dark room cannot be seen, but shines when a torch falls on it. The Moon is like the plate, and the Sun is like the torch.
explanations.context: This card says where the Moon's light comes from.
explanations.art: The Sun on the left, the Earth in the middle with a child on the night side, and the Moon above, its sunny side glowing, with arrows from the Sun to the Moon and from the Moon to the child.

explanations.concept: The stars are faraway suns, in different colours
explanations.definition: Every star is a sun, a huge ball of very hot gas that makes its own light. Stars look like tiny dots because they are very far away.
explanations.description: The Sun is our nearest star. The other stars are so far away that their light takes years to reach us. Bright stars have colours: reddish stars are the coolest, and bluish white stars are the hottest.
examples: Thiruvathirai, also called Ardra, is a bright reddish orange star in the winter evening sky.
Sirius, the brightest star at night, looks bluish white and often twinkles in many colours when low.
A gas flame is blue where it is hottest, and a dying coal glows red.
explanations.context: This card says what stars are, and why they have colours.
explanations.art: A dark sky with one reddish orange star and one bluish white star, and a small Sun drawn beside them as one more star.

explanations.concept: Stars twinkle, and planets usually shine steadily
explanations.definition: Starlight flickers because the moving air above us bends it this way and that. Planets usually shine more steadily.
explanations.description: Starlight passes through a thick blanket of moving air before it reaches us, and the air wobbles it. A star is so far away that its light is one tiny point, so the wobble makes it flicker. A planet looks like a tiny round patch, not a single point. The wobbles in different parts of the patch mostly cancel out, so the planet shines steadily. Planets also wander slowly among the stars from week to week.
examples: Stars low down near the rooftops twinkle more, because their light passes through more air.
Jupiter usually shines steadily, like a calm lamp.
Astronauts in space see the stars shine steadily, with no twinkle.
explanations.context: This card explains why stars twinkle.
explanations.art: A star with flicker marks and a steady planet dot in the sky, and wavy lines of moving air between them and a child below.

agreed.text: The Moon makes no light of its own. It shines with sunlight.
agreed.evidence: The bright side of the Moon always faces the Sun. Spacecraft such as India's Chandrayaan have photographed the Moon up close: grey rock and dust, with no fire or lamp.

agreed.text: Stars are suns, very far away.
agreed.evidence: The light from stars, split into its colours, looks like the Sun's light. Astronomers have measured how far away many stars are. Even the nearest one after the Sun is so far that its light takes over four years to reach us.

agreed.text: Planets move slowly among the stars.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can watch a planet for a few weeks and see it change its place among the stars. People in India, China, Babylon and Greece recorded this thousands of years ago. The Greek word planet means wanderer.

challenging.claim: The Moon follows me wherever I go.
challenging.who: A common idea among young children, and a feeling many grown-ups still have
challenging.for: From a moving bus or car, the Moon really does seem to keep up with the window.
challenging.against: In the window strip test, near things slid past and the Moon stayed put. Someone in another city sees the same Moon at the same moment (try the One Moon, Two Windows project). The Moon is so far that it seems to keep up with everyone at once.
challenging.context: This card is about the Moon following you.

challenging.claim: Stars twinkle because they blink on and off.
challenging.who: A common idea among young children
challenging.for: A twinkling star really does seem to flash and flicker.
challenging.against: In the hot tawa test, the torch made a steady light, but it shivered when seen through moving warm air. Stars shine steadily too. Astronauts above the air see them without any twinkle.
challenging.context: This card is about why stars twinkle.

challenging.claim: Every bright dot in the night sky is a star.
challenging.who: A common idea among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Venus, Jupiter and an aeroplane can all look like bright stars.
challenging.against: Some bright dots are planets that shine with sunlight and hardly twinkle. Some move steadily and blink red and green: those are aeroplanes.
challenging.context: This card is about bright dots in the night sky.

big_questions.q: In the window strip test, the paper strips slid past when you walked, and the Moon stayed in the same place. How could you use this to tell which of two lights is farther away?
big_questions.hint: Walk a few steps and watch which light slides more against the sky.

big_questions.q: In the hot tawa test, the light never changed, but it looked as if it did. When a star twinkles, is the star changing, or is it the air, or is it you?
big_questions.hint: In the hot tawa test, think about what changed when the stove was switched off.

big_questions.q: A dung beetle, some birds and people all use the night sky to find their way. What do you think the sky looks like to them?
big_questions.hint: Each animal has different eyes. A beetle may see the glow of the Milky Way as one bright stripe.

big_questions.q: A planet moves slowly among the stars from week to week. How could you check that a bright dot is a planet, with no gadget?
big_questions.hint: Mark where the dot is next to a rooftop or a star, and look again after a week.

story.title: The Moon on the Night Bus
story.note: Nila is a Tamil word for the Moon. Paati means grandmother in Tamil. Nila, Paati, Appa and Meher are made up. Guwahati is in Assam, far away in the northeast of India, but its sky has the same Moon.
text: Nila was six. She lived in a flat in Chennai with her Appa and her grandmother, Paati.
One night they were coming home on the bus from a wedding in Tambaram. Nila had the window seat. She pressed her nose to the glass.
Outside, everything was rushing past. Street lamps went whoosh, whoosh, whoosh. A tea shop flashed by, then a tall tree, then a petrol pump with bright lights.
But up above the rooftops, there was the Moon. She was half round, like a broken appalam, and she was not rushing at all. She kept pace with the bus, right beside Nila's window.
"Paati," whispered Nila. "The Moon is following us."
Paati leaned over and looked. "Is she? Keep watching. Tell me what she does when the bus turns."
The bus turned left at a big junction. The Moon slid round to the other window. The bus turned again. The Moon came back. When the bus stopped at a signal, the Moon stopped too.
"She waits for us!" said Nila. "She must like us."
Paati smiled. "Maybe she likes everybody," she said. "Tomorrow, let's find out."
The next evening, Paati called Nila to the window of their flat. She had stuck three strips of paper on the glass, a hand-width apart. She had put one slipper on the floor at each end of the window.
"Stand at the first slipper," said Paati. "Close one eye. Where is the Moon?"
"Just next to the first strip," said Nila.
"Now walk slowly to the other slipper. Keep watching."
Nila walked. The strips slid across the Moon, one, two, three. The water tank on the next building slid a little. But the Moon stayed exactly where she was, high over the rooftops.
"The strips moved and the Moon didn't!" said Nila. "But the strips are stuck on the glass. They can't move."

"That's right," said Paati. "Only you moved. Near things look as if they slide past when you move. Far things hardly change. The Moon is very, very far away. If we could drive there without stopping, it would take more than six months."
Just then Paati's phone rang. It was Nila's cousin Meher, calling from Guwahati, a long, long way away.
"Meher," said Paati, "go to your window. Can you see the Moon?"
Meher ran to look. She held up the phone. There was a dark sky, a bamboo pole, and a half Moon, exactly like Nila's.
"It's the same Moon!" said Nila. "She's at your window and at my window, at the same time!"
"She is," said Paati. "She is not following you, and not following Meher. She is so far away that she looks the same to everyone. So everyone thinks she came along with them."
Nila thought about it. Then she frowned. "But she was so bright last night. Is she a big lamp?"
"The Moon is made of grey rock," said Paati. "She has no light of her own. The Sun shines on her, even at night, from the other side of the Earth. We see the sunlight bouncing off her."
Later, Appa came home from work. He found Nila waiting at the door.
"Appa, come to the window," she said. "I'll show you why the Moon follows the bus."
She made him stand at the first slipper and close one eye. She made him walk slowly to the other slipper.
"The strips slide," said Appa, surprised. "The Moon stays."
"Because she's very, very far," said Nila. "So she goes with everyone at once. Even with Meher in Guwahati."
Appa looked at the Moon for a long time. "When I was small, in my village, I thought she followed only me," he said.
"She seemed to," said Nila. "And she seemed to follow everyone else too."
story.epiphany: For the parent: Nila finds that the paper strips on the glass slide past the Moon when she walks, while the Moon stays in the same place. Near things change place when we move, but the Moon is so far away that she hardly changes place at all. So the Moon seems to follow everyone at once. Nila sees this when her cousin in Guwahati shows the same Moon on the phone. Nila then teaches her Appa.
ask: Why did the Moon seem to follow the bus, while the street lamps rushed past?
What did the paper strips do when Nila walked past the window? What did the Moon do?
How could Nila and Meher both see the Moon at their own windows at the same time?
Where does the Moon's light come from?
art: A girl in a bus window seat at night, street lamps streaking past outside, and a half Moon still above the rooftops.
A grandmother and a girl at a flat window with three paper strips on the glass and a slipper on the floor at each end.
The girl holding a phone showing her cousin's window in Guwahati with a bamboo pole and the same half Moon.
The girl showing her father how to walk past the window with one eye closed, the Moon outside.

experiments.title: Does the Moon Follow You? The window strip test
experiments.context: In this experiment you walk past a window and watch the Moon. You find out if the Moon really comes along with you.
experiments.question: When you walk, do near things and the faraway Moon seem to move in the same way?
experiments.predict: When you walk past the window, will the Moon slide away like the paper strips, or stay with you? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We walk the same path each time, between two slippers. We keep our head at the same height, and close the same eye, so only our steps change what we see.
results_table: Did it slide when I walked?

materials.item: a steel tumbler
a stool or a chair
strips of paper, about as long as your hand
sticky tape, or a little cooked rice to stick the strips
two slippers, to mark where to start and stop
a window or a balcony from which you can see the Moon
paper and crayons

experiments.safety: On a balcony, stay well back from the railing. Never climb on a chair or a ledge to see the Moon. A grown-up stays beside the child.

schedule.what: Try the tumbler test in a room, guess what the Moon will do, then walk past a window and watch the Moon.

experiments.record: Draw the window, the three strips and the Moon. Draw an arrow on each thing that slid. A grown-up writes 'near' or 'far' beside each one.

setup.art: A steel tumbler on a stool in a room, a calendar on the far wall behind it, and a girl three steps away with one eye closed.
setup.caption: 1. Look at a tumbler in front of a far wall. Take two steps to the side.

setup.art: A window at night with three paper strips stuck on the glass, a hand-width apart, and the Moon outside near the first strip.
setup.caption: 2. Stick three paper strips on the window glass, near where the Moon shows.

setup.art: Two slippers on the floor along the window, about three steps apart, and a girl standing at the first one with one eye closed.
setup.caption: 3. Stand at one slipper. Close one eye. Find the Moon.

setup.art: The girl halfway between the slippers, the strips now on the other side of the Moon, and the Moon in the same place in the sky.
setup.caption: 4. Walk slowly to the other slipper. Watch the strips and the Moon.

flow.do: 1. Put a steel tumbler on a stool in the middle of a room. 2. Your child stands three big steps away. 3. The tumbler should be in front of something on the far wall, such as a calendar.
flow.say: Close one eye. Is the tumbler in front of the calendar? Now take two big steps to the side. Where is the tumbler now?
flow.kid: Close one eye. Look at the tumbler and the calendar. Take two big steps sideways. Look again.

good: The tumbler moved away from the calendar.
The near tumbler slid, and the far wall stayed.

flow.parent: Nothing moved except your child. The near tumbler seems to jump across the far wall. Don't explain yet. Let your child notice it and say it in their own words.

flow.do: Tell your child about tonight's test. Ask for a guess and a reason. A grown-up writes both down in the table.
flow.say: Tonight we will walk past the window and watch the Moon. Will the Moon slide away, like the tumbler? Or will it come with you? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Will the Moon slide away, or come with you? Why do you think so?

ask.q: What will the Moon do, and why?
good: It will come with me, because it follows our car.
It will slide, like the tumbler did.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Most children of six say the Moon will come with them. Don't say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. After dark, find a window or balcony where you can see the Moon. 2. Stick three paper strips on the glass, a hand-width apart, near the Moon. 3. Put a slipper at each end of a three-step path.
flow.say: Stand at this slipper. Close one eye. Is the Moon to the left or the right of the first strip?
flow.kid: Stand at the slipper. Close one eye. Find the Moon. Where is it next to the strips?
flow.parent: Pick an evening when the Moon is up (see the Look Closely at the Moon activity). A calendar that shows Purnima helps. If you cannot see the Moon, use the brightest dot in the sky. It works the same way. On a balcony, you can watch the grill bars instead of paper strips.

flow.do: 1. Your child walks slowly to the other slipper, one eye closed, watching the Moon. 2. Then they walk back. 3. Ask them to watch a far building or water tank too.
flow.say: Walk slowly to the other slipper. Keep watching the Moon. What do the strips do? What does the Moon do? What does that far building do?
flow.kid: Walk slowly. Watch the Moon and the strips. What slides? What stays?

good: The strips slid past the Moon.
The far building slid a little.
The Moon stayed in the same place.

flow.parent: Look for three things. The strips slide past fast, because they are near. A far building slides a little. The Moon does not seem to move at all. If the strips seem to jump about, your child may be opening both eyes. Try again with one eye covered by a hand.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they thought, what they saw, and why. 2. Then explain, using what they saw.
flow.say: Was your guess right? What did the strips do? Why do you think the Moon stayed? Near things slide past when we move. The Moon is so far away that our steps make no difference.
flow.kid: Was your guess right? Near things slide past when you move. The Moon is very far. So it stays.

check.q: When you walked past the window, what slid past the most?
options: The paper strips on the glass
check.why: The strips were the nearest, so they slid the most. The far building slid a little, and the Moon not at all. If your child picks the Moon, they still feel that the Moon follows the bus. Try the walk once more and watch only the Moon.

flow.parent: Now link it to the bus. From a bus, the lamp posts are near, so they rush past. The Moon is so far that the bus ride hardly changes where it is. So it seems to come along.

experiments.title: Why Do Stars Twinkle? The hot tawa test
experiments.context: In this experiment you look at a small light through the warm air above a hot dosa tawa. You find out what makes a star twinkle. It needs the stove, so do it when a grown-up can use the kitchen.
experiments.question: Does a small, steady light shiver when we look at it through moving warm air?
experiments.predict: We will look at a small light across a hot tawa. Will the light stay steady, or will it shiver? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We look at the same small light, from the same place, with our eyes at the height of the tawa. We look once with the tawa cold and once with it hot, so only the air above it changes.
results_table: Did the small light stay steady or shiver?

materials.item: an iron dosa tawa, or a steel pan (not a non-stick one)
a gas or electric stove
a small light, such as a phone torch or a small LED lamp
a steel box or a few upturned steel plates to stand the phone on

experiments.safety: Only a grown-up lights the stove and handles the tawa. The child stands back, at least two big steps from the stove, and never touches the tawa. Keep dupattas, sleeves and paper away from the flame. Switch the stove off as soon as the test is done.

schedule.what: Look at a small light across a cold tawa, then across a hot one, and compare.

experiments.record: Draw the small light with straight lines when the tawa was cold, and with wiggly lines when it was hot.

setup.art: A kitchen counter with a cold iron tawa on the stove, a phone torch shining on a steel box just behind it, and a girl two big steps back with her eyes at tawa height.
setup.caption: 1. Put a small light just behind the tawa. Look across the cold tawa.

setup.art: The same kitchen, the grown-up's hand turning the stove knob on, and wavy lines of warm air rising from the tawa in front of the light.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up heats the tawa for two minutes.

setup.art: The girl looking across the hot tawa at the small light, the light drawn with little shiver marks around it.
setup.caption: 3. Look across the hot tawa again. What does the light do?

flow.do: 1. Stand the phone on the steel box, a forearm's length behind the tawa, with its torch on. 2. Your child stands two big steps back. 3. They crouch so their eyes are at tawa height.
flow.say: Look across the tawa at the little light. Is it steady, or does it shiver?
flow.kid: Crouch down. Look across the tawa at the little light. Is it steady?
flow.parent: The tawa is still cold. The light should look steady. Point the torch at the ceiling or the wall, not into your child's eyes.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason before you heat the tawa. A grown-up writes it in the table.
flow.say: I will heat the tawa. The light will stay just the same. Will it still look steady, or will it shiver? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The tawa will get hot. Will the light shiver? Why do you think so?

good: It will stay steady, because the light is the same.
It will shiver, because of the heat.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Don't say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Heat the tawa on a medium flame for about two minutes, as you would before making dosa. 2. Your child looks across it again, from the same place.
flow.say: Look across the hot tawa at the little light. What is the light doing now?
flow.kid: Stay back. Look across the hot tawa. What does the light do?

good: The light is shivering.
It is wobbling and dancing.
The things behind the tawa are wobbly.

flow.parent: Warm air rises from the tawa in moving swirls. Light bends a little as it passes through warm and cool air, so the small light seems to shiver and dance. The shiver is small and quick, but you can see it. If you cannot, heat the tawa a minute longer and crouch lower, so your eyes are level with the tawa.

flow.do: 1. Switch off the stove. 2. Look again after one or two minutes, while the tawa cools. Do not touch it.
flow.say: The stove is off now. Look again. Is the light still shivering?
flow.kid: The stove is off. Look again. Is the light still shivering?
flow.parent: As the tawa cools, the shivering gets weaker. A hot tawa stays hot for a long time, so keep everyone's hands away.

flow.do: Ask what your child thought, what they saw, and why. Then link it to the stars.
flow.say: Did the light change? Or did the air change? The air above us moves all the time, like the air over the tawa. It makes starlight shiver. That is twinkling.
flow.kid: The light stayed the same. The moving warm air made it shiver. Moving air makes stars twinkle too.

check.q: In the hot tawa test, what made the little light shiver?
options: The moving warm air above the tawa
The phone torch switching on and off
check.why: The torch made the same steady light all the time. The warm air rising from the tawa bent its light this way and that. If your child picks 'switching on and off', the shiver looked like blinking to them. Switch off the stove and watch the light go steady again.

activities.title: Look Closely at the Moon: draw its face
activities.context: In this activity you look at the Moon from your window for a few minutes, and draw its shape and its dark patches.

materials.item: a window or balcony from which you can see the Moon
paper and a grey or black crayon

activities.safety: On a balcony, stay well back from the railing.

setup.art: A girl and a grown-up at a flat window at night, the room light off, looking at a bright Moon with grey patches.
setup.caption: 1. Switch off the room light. Look at the Moon for a while.

setup.art: A child's drawing of the Moon's shape with grey patches shaded in, and a small rabbit shape drawn beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the Moon's shape and its dark patches.

flow.do: 1. After dark, switch off the room light. 2. Stand at a window with your child where you can see the Moon. 3. Look at it quietly together.
flow.say: Look at the Moon. What do you notice? What shape is it tonight? Can you see any dark patches?
flow.kid: Look at the Moon. What shape is it? Can you see dark patches?

ask.q: What do you notice about the Moon?
good: It is half round tonight.
It has grey patches.
It is very bright.

flow.parent: The Moon is up in the evening for about two weeks of each month, from the thin new Moon to the full Moon. If it is not up tonight, try another evening, or look for it in the morning sky after Purnima.

flow.do: Your child draws the Moon's shape and shades in the dark patches. Ask what the patches look like to them.
flow.say: Draw the Moon's shape. Shade the dark patches. What do the patches look like to you? The dark patches are flat plains of old, dark rock.
flow.kid: Draw the Moon's shape. Shade the dark patches. What do they look like?
flow.parent: Many people in India see a rabbit in the patches. Others see a face, or a woman with a pot. Any answer is fine. Keep the drawing for the window strip test.

activities.title: Twinkle or Steady? Find a planet
activities.context: In this activity you look at bright dots in the evening sky. You find out which ones twinkle and which shine steadily.

materials.item: a window or balcony with a view of the sky
a phone with a free sky map, such as Stellarium Web, if you have one

activities.safety: On a balcony, stay well back from the railing.

setup.art: A boy at a balcony at dusk pointing at two dots: one with flicker marks around it, and one bright, steady dot low in the orange sky.
setup.caption: 1. Find two or three bright dots. Watch each one while you count to ten.

setup.art: A child's paper with two columns, 'twinkles' and 'steady', and a drawn dot in each.
setup.caption: 2. Sort them: twinkles, or steady?

flow.do: 1. In the early evening, look for the brightest dots in the sky. 2. Pick two or three. 3. Your child watches each one while counting slowly to ten.
flow.say: Look at that bright dot. Count to ten with me. Does it flicker and shiver, or shine steadily?
flow.kid: Look at one bright dot. Count to ten. Does it flicker, or stay steady?
flow.parent: A very bright, steady dot low in the west just after sunset, or in the east before sunrise, is often Venus. Its name is Shukra in Sanskrit and Velli in Tamil. Another bright, steady dot may be Jupiter. A free sky map such as Stellarium Web shows which planets are up tonight. Dots very low near the rooftops twinkle more, even planets. If you see no steady dot tonight, that is fine: you still saw which dots twinkle. Try another evening.

flow.do: Your child draws each dot in a 'twinkles' column or a 'steady' column. Then tell them what the steady ones might be.
flow.say: Which dots twinkled? Which were steady? The steady ones may be planets. A planet shines with sunlight, like the Moon.
flow.kid: Draw the dots that twinkled, and the steady ones. Steady dots may be planets.

ask.q: Why might the steady dot be a planet?
good: Planets usually don't twinkle.
Stars twinkle, and that one didn't.

activities.title: Roll Like a Dung Beetle
activities.context: In this activity you roll a paper ball across a room, once with your eyes open and once with them shut. You find out why a dung beetle watches the night sky.

materials.item: an old newspaper, scrunched into a ball
a torch or a lamp, at the far end of the room
a clear floor, with nothing to trip on

setup.art: A girl on her hands and knees pushing a newspaper ball across a floor towards a lit torch on a stool, her path drawn as a straight line.
setup.caption: 1. Roll the ball towards the torch, eyes open.

setup.art: The same girl rolling the ball with her eyes shut, her path drawn as a curly, wandering line, a grown-up walking beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Roll it again with your eyes shut. Where does it go?

flow.do: Tell your child about the dung beetle.
flow.say: In Africa, a dung beetle rolls a ball of dung away to eat. At night, the beetle rolls it in a straight line. Scientists found the beetle watches the sky to do it.
flow.kid: A dung beetle rolls a ball at night. The beetle keeps a straight line by watching the sky.

flow.do: 1. Put the lit torch on a stool at the far end of the room. 2. Your child pushes the paper ball towards it on hands and knees, eyes open.
flow.say: Push your ball towards the light, like a beetle. Keep your eyes on the light.
flow.kid: Push your ball to the light. Keep looking at the light.

flow.do: 1. Start again from the same place. 2. Your child shuts their eyes and pushes the ball again. 3. Walk beside them so they don't bump into anything.
flow.say: Now close your eyes and roll the ball to the light again. Stop when I say stop.
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Roll the ball to the light. Stop when told.
flow.parent: Most children curve away or go in circles within a few metres.

flow.do: Talk about what happened, and about the real beetles.
flow.say: Which time did you go straight? In 2013, the scientist Marie Dacke and her team tested this with dung beetles. When the beetles could see the starry sky, they rolled straight. When the sky was hidden, they wandered.
flow.kid: Eyes open, you went straight. Eyes shut, you wandered. Beetles need the sky too.

games.title: Moon, Star, Planet or Plane? A sorting card game
games.players: 2 or more: a grown-up reads the cards, and one or more children play.
games.context: This is a card game. A grown-up reads a card about something in the sky, and you say what it is.

items.f: A big round light that changes shape over the month
items.b: MOON paper. It shines with sunlight.

items.f: A dot that twinkles and shivers
items.b: STAR paper. Stars make their own light.

items.f: A very bright dot, steady, low in the west just after sunset
items.b: PLANET paper. Probably Venus, shining with sunlight.

items.f: A light that moves across the sky and blinks red and green
items.b: OTHER paper. It is an aeroplane, with its own lamps.

items.f: A thin curved shape like a fingernail, just after sunset
items.b: MOON paper. A thin crescent Moon.

items.f: A bright steady dot that slowly changes its place among the stars over many weeks
items.b: PLANET paper. Planets wander among the stars.

items.f: Seven stars in the shape of a ladle
items.b: STAR paper. These stars are the Saptarishi.

items.f: The biggest, brightest light, seen only in the day
items.b: STAR paper. The Sun is our nearest star. Never look straight at it.

items.f: A pale, rocky ball you can sometimes see in the daytime sky
items.b: MOON paper. The Moon is often up in the day too.

items.f: A steady dot that glides smoothly across the sky in a few minutes, with no blinking
items.b: OTHER paper. It is the space station, with people living in it. It shines with sunlight, like a planet.

items.f: A tiny dot that looks reddish and steady
items.b: PLANET paper. It may be Mars.

items.f: A streak of light that flashes across the sky in one second
items.b: OTHER paper. A shooting star is really a tiny grain of space dust burning up in the air. It is not a star.

items.f: A bright dot that twinkles in many colours, very low near the rooftops
items.b: STAR paper. Low stars twinkle the most.

items.f: A round, lit face with grey patches on it
items.b: MOON paper. You can see these grey patches with your eyes alone.

items.f: A very bright, steady dot high up at midnight
items.b: PLANET paper. Maybe Jupiter, Saturn or Mars. Venus is never up at midnight.

items.f: A red light on top of a tall tower that blinks but never moves
items.b: OTHER paper. It is a warning lamp on a tower, for aeroplanes. It is not in the sky.

rules: Mix the 16 cards and put them in a pile, face down.
Lay four papers on the floor: MOON, STAR, PLANET and OTHER. Draw a Moon, a twinkling star, a steady dot and an aeroplane on them.
Players take turns. On your turn, a grown-up reads the front of the top card.
Put the card on the paper you think is right, and say why.
Turn the card over and read the back. If the paper is right, keep the card. If not, put it to one side.
When the pile is finished, count your cards. With two or more children, the most cards wins, and a tie is a shared win. With one child, the goal is 12 cards or more.

setup.art: Four papers on the floor with drawings of a Moon, a twinkling star, a steady planet dot and an aeroplane, and a pile of cards beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the four papers: Moon, Star, Planet, Other.

setup.art: A girl putting a card on the PLANET paper while a grown-up turns another card over to read the back.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Put it on a paper. Turn it over to check.

flow.do: Lay out the four papers. Read the rules together.
flow.say: Each card tells you about a light in the sky. You say if it is the Moon, a star, a planet or something else.
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Is it the Moon, a star, a planet, or other?

flow.do: Play through all 16 cards, taking turns. Read each front, wait for the choice and reason, then read the back.
flow.say: A dot that twinkles and shivers. Moon, star, planet or other? Why? Let's turn it over.
flow.kid: Listen. Which paper? Why? Turn it over and check.
flow.parent: The tricky cards are the steady dots, the space station and the shooting star. Ask: does it twinkle? Does it move? Does it make its own light?

flow.do: Find the red tower lamp card and read it again.
flow.say: A red light blinks on a tall tower, but it never moves. Is it a star in the sky?
flow.kid: A red light blinks on a tower and never moves. Is it a star?

check.q: A red light blinks on top of a tall tower and never moves. Is it a star?
options: No, it is a lamp on the tower
Yes, it is a star that blinks
check.why: A lamp on a tower is not in the sky. It warns aeroplanes. A star would twinkle high up, and would not stay on top of a tower.

games.title: Twinkle, Steady, Fly! A moving game
games.players: 2 or more players: one caller and the rest movers.
games.context: This is a moving game. The caller shows a card, and the movers act out a star, a planet, an aeroplane or the Moon.

items.f: STAR!
items.b: Stand still and twinkle your fingers above your head.

items.f: PLANET!
items.b: Stand still with your arms in a round circle. Do not twinkle. Shine steadily.

items.f: AEROPLANE!
items.b: Walk across the room with your arms out, blinking your eyes.

items.f: MOON!
items.b: Make a big circle with your arms and stay still while the caller walks around you.

items.f: HOT AIR!
items.b: First shiver your whole body, like a star in moving air. Then sway only a tiny bit, like a planet.

items.f: LIGHT ON THE MOON!
items.b: A grown-up holds a torch or lamp, as the Sun. Stand like the Moon, with your arms in a circle, and turn your face to the light. The side facing the light is the lit side.

items.f: SHOOTING STAR!
items.b: Zoom one hand fast across the sky and say 'whoosh'.

items.f: CLOUDS!
items.b: Everyone crouches down and covers their face.

rules: One player is the caller. The caller holds the call cards.
At the start, the caller reads the back of each card aloud once, so everyone knows the moves.
The caller reads the front of a card out loud. Everyone else does the move, as fast as they can.
Anyone who does the wrong move, such as twinkling for PLANET, becomes the next caller. The caller also changes after every four calls.
If the cards run out, shuffle them and go on. Play until everyone has been the caller once. There is no winner: it is a game to move and laugh.

setup.art: A grown-up holding up a card that says STAR, and two children twinkling their fingers above their heads.
setup.caption: 1. The caller reads a card.

setup.art: A girl standing still with her arms in a round circle while another child walks around her.
setup.caption: 2. Everyone acts it out.

flow.do: Read the back of each call card aloud once, and show the move.
flow.say: Here are the moves. A star twinkles. A planet shines steadily. An aeroplane flies and blinks.
flow.kid: Learn the moves. Star twinkles. Planet stays steady. Plane flies and blinks.

flow.do: Play. Call the cards in any order, faster and faster.
flow.say: Planet! Moon! Star! Hot air! Who shivers the most?
flow.kid: Listen for the call. Do the move fast!
flow.parent: At HOT AIR, ask: why do stars shiver more than planets? A star's light comes from one tiny point, so moving air shakes it more. At MOON, walk round the Moon player. The Moon player stands still, as the real Moon seems to stay put when we move.

flow.do: End with one question.
flow.say: When you walked round the Moon player, the Moon player stood still. What does that remind you of?
flow.kid: The Moon player stood still while we walked round. What does that remind you of?

ask.q: What does the Moon player standing still remind you of?
good: The Moon seems to stay in the same place when we move.
The Moon looks the same to everyone.

projects.title: One Moon, Two Windows
projects.context: In this project you phone someone who lives in another town. You both look at the Moon at the same time, and draw it.

materials.item: a phone
a relative or friend in another town who can look at the sky (or a friend in another part of your own city)
paper and crayons

schedule.what: Phone someone in another town. Both look at the Moon at the same time and draw it.
Compare the two drawings. Then do it again on another evening.

projects.record: Stick your drawing and the other person's drawing side by side. Write the two town names and the time.

setup.art: A girl at a flat window in Kochi talking on a phone, looking at a half Moon.
setup.caption: 1. Phone someone in another town. Both look at the Moon.

setup.art: Two drawings of a half Moon side by side, labelled with two town names and the same time.
setup.caption: 2. Compare the two drawings.

flow.do: 1. Choose an evening when the Moon is up. 2. Phone a relative or friend in another town. 3. Ask them to look for the Moon at the same time.
flow.say: Let's call a relative or friend in another town. We will both look at the Moon at the same time.
flow.kid: Call someone far away. Ask them to look at the Moon now.

flow.do: 1. Both of you draw the Moon's shape. 2. Ask them to draw it too, and send a photo.
flow.say: Draw the Moon's shape. Is it round, half or thin? Ask your friend what their Moon looks like.
flow.kid: Draw the Moon's shape. Ask what their Moon looks like.

flow.do: Put the two drawings side by side.
flow.say: Look at both drawings. Are they the same shape? How can one Moon be at both windows at once?
flow.kid: Look at both drawings. Are they the same? How can that be?

good: It is the same Moon.
The Moon is so far away that everyone sees it the same.

flow.do: Do it again on another evening, with someone in a different town if you can.
flow.say: Let's try again with someone else. Will their Moon match ours too?
flow.kid: Try again with someone else. Will it match?
flow.parent: Everyone in India sees the same shape of Moon on the same night. If you have no one in another town, call a friend in another part of your own city.

challenges.title: Show That the Moon Is Not Following the Scooter
challenges.context: This is a problem to solve. A grandfather says the Moon follows his scooter home. How can you show him why it only seems to?
challenges.problem: A grandfather says the Moon follows his scooter all the way home. How can you show him, at home, why the Moon only seems to follow him?
constraints: Use only things you already have at home.
Do it inside the flat, or at a window.
The grandfather must be able to see it for himself, not just hear it.
general: Do the window strip test with him: near strips slide past, and the Moon stays put.
Ask him to watch the lamp posts and the Moon from the seat of a bus or car, when someone else is driving.
Phone someone in another town and ask them where their Moon is.
creative: Put a torch on a stool at the far end of a long corridor as a pretend Moon. Walk past near things and watch the torch stay put.
Ask him to point at the Moon from one end of the balcony, then from the other end. His arm points the same way both times.
Make a little play: one person is a lamp post, one walks past like the scooter, and a far wall is the Moon.
challenges.your_turn: Choose one idea and show it to a grown-up. Did they see why the Moon only seems to follow us? What would you change to make it clearer?

setup.art: A girl at a window with a grown-up, pointing at paper strips on the glass and the Moon outside.
setup.caption: 1. Think of a way to show the grandfather, at home.

setup.art: A grown-up walking past the window with one eye closed, the girl watching and smiling.
setup.caption: 2. Show him. Did he see it?

flow.do: Read the problem to your child. Ask what they could show the grown-up.
flow.say: A grandfather thinks the Moon follows his scooter. How could you show him why it only seems to?
flow.kid: A grandfather thinks the Moon follows his scooter. How could you show him?

good: The window strip test.
The tumbler and the far wall.
Phoning someone far away.

flow.do: Let your child set up their idea and show it to another grown-up. Help only if asked.
flow.say: Show your idea. Ask them what they see. Can they say why the Moon seems to follow?
flow.kid: Show your idea. Ask what they see.
flow.parent: The best ideas let the grown-up see near things slide past while a far thing stays put. Let your child do the explaining.

flow.do: Talk about how it went.
flow.say: Did your idea work? What would you change to make it clearer?
flow.kid: Did it work? What would you change?

videos.title: Dung beetles navigate using the stars
videos.why: Shows the real beetles that Marie Dacke's team studied, finding their way using the Milky Way.
videos.check: Found by search: "Dung Beetles Navigate Using the Stars" by Science Channel, 1 minute 48 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: The Moon seen through a telescope: craters and dark plains
videos.why: Shows that the Moon is grey rock, lit by the Sun, with no light of its own.
videos.check: Find a real telescope video of the Moon from an observatory, a planetarium or an amateur astronomer. Check it says the Moon shines with sunlight.

videos.title: India's Chandrayaan-3 makes a historic Moon landing
videos.why: Shows news of Indian scientists landing on the Moon on 23 August 2023, near its south pole.
videos.check: Found by search: "India's Chandrayaan-3 makes historic moon landing" by Guardian News, 1 minute 46 seconds. A parent may preview it.

quiz.p: From a moving bus, the street lamps rush past. What does the Moon seem to do?
quiz.why: The Moon is so far away that the bus ride hardly changes where you see it, so it seems to come along.

quiz.p: You take two steps sideways. A steel tumbler on a stool seems to jump across the far wall. Why?
opts: The tumbler is near you, so a few steps change where you see it
quiz.why: Near things seem to move a lot when you move, and far things hardly move at all. Only you moved.

quiz.p: One person in Chennai and another in Guwahati look up at the night sky at the same time. What do they see?
opts: Only the person in Guwahati can see the Moon
quiz.why: There is one Moon. It is so far away that people all over India see it at the same time.

quiz.p: Where does the Moon's light come from?
quiz.why: The Moon is grey rock with no light of its own. Sunlight falls on it and bounces to us.

quiz.p: Which of these makes its own light?
quiz.why: A star is a sun. Venus is a planet, and Venus and the Moon shine only with sunlight.

quiz.p: Why do stars close to the rooftops twinkle more than stars high up?
opts: Their light goes through more air
quiz.why: The light of a low star passes through more of the moving air before it reaches us, so it shivers more.

quiz.p: Where would a star look steady, with no twinkle at all?
opts: From a spacecraft above the air
From a balcony on a windy night
quiz.why: Twinkling comes from the moving air. Above the air, in space, stars shine steadily.

quiz.p: You see a bright dot in the night sky that does not twinkle at all. What could it be?
quiz.why: Stars usually twinkle. Planets usually shine steadily, because their light comes from a tiny round patch, not a single point.
The air above us is always moving. It bends starlight this way and that, so the star seems to flicker.

quiz.p: A light moves across the night sky and blinks red and green. What is it?
quiz.why: Aeroplanes have blinking red and green lamps, and they move across the sky quickly. Planets and the Moon don't blink.

items.p: A grown-up reads each one. Does it make its own light, or shine with sunlight? Colour the ones that make their own light yellow.
items.why: The Sun and the other stars make their own light. The Moon and the planets, such as Venus and Jupiter, only shine because sunlight falls on them.

items.p: You walk past your window and watch the Moon and the paper strips on the glass. What slides past?
items.why: The strips are near, so they slide past when you walk. The Moon is very far, so it stays in the same place.

items.p: Stars twinkle because they blink on and off by themselves.
items.why: False. A steady light shivers when it shines through moving warm air, as the hot tawa test shows. The moving air above us makes starlight shiver in the same way.

items.p: Draw the Moon as you saw it from your window. Shade in its dark patches.
items.a: The Moon's shape that night, with grey patches shaded in.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the shape the child really saw, with the dark patches shaded.
items.art: An empty window frame with a dark sky inside it.

items.p: Draw a line from what you see to what it is.
pairs: A bright dot that shines steadily
A light that moves and blinks red and green
A big round light with grey patches
items.why: Stars usually twinkle. Planets usually shine steadily. Aeroplanes move and blink. The Moon is big and round, with grey patches of rock.
items.art: On the left, four small pictures: a twinkling dot, a steady dot, a blinking aeroplane light and a Moon. On the right, the four names.

items.p: Draw the window, one paper strip on the glass, and the Moon. Then draw where the strip looks to be after you walk to the other slipper. Draw an arrow for the way it slid.
items.a: The strip drawn in two places with an arrow between them, and the Moon in the same place both times.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the near strip changing place and the far Moon staying where it is.
items.art: An empty window frame with one paper strip stuck on the glass and a Moon outside.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: you are on a moving train. Outside the window you see the poles by the track, the far hills and the Moon. Which one seems to move fastest, and which hardly moves? Why?
items.a: The poles seem to rush past, the far hills move slowly, and the Moon hardly moves. Near things change place the most, and the Moon is the farthest.
items.why: A strong answer puts the poles, hills and Moon in order of how near they are, and says near things seem to move more.

items.p: Three people are looking at the Moon. They have different ideas about whether the Moon is a light.

views.says: The Moon is a light. It lights up the road at night.
The Moon is not a light source. Its light comes from the Sun.
You are both right in a way. The Moon helps us see, but the light started at the Sun.

items.ask: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it: who do you agree with most? Why? Then say one good thing about someone else's idea.
items.a: Any choice with a good reason. Farhana is right that moonlight helps us see. Meenakshi is right that the Moon makes no light of its own. Ammamma joins both ideas.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason, and fairly says what is good about another view. Moonlight is real light that helps us see, and it all started at the Sun.

items.p: Look at this night sky. A grown-up points to each thing. Say what it is, and the grown-up writes it.
items.why: The big round light is the Moon. A twinkling dot is a star. A steady bright dot is probably a planet. A light that moves and blinks is an aeroplane.
items.art: A night sky over flat rooftops with a big Moon, a twinkling star, a steady bright dot and a blinking aeroplane, each with an empty label.

items.p: Look at this night sky picture. Count the dots that twinkle. Then count the dots that shine steadily.
items.a: 5 twinkle and 2 are steady. The steady ones are probably planets.
items.why: Stars usually twinkle, and planets usually shine steadily. So the 2 steady dots are probably planets.
items.art: A night sky over rooftops with exactly 7 dots: 5 drawn with little flicker marks around them, and 2 drawn as plain round steady dots.

items.p: Number these from 1 to 4, in the order you see them on a clear evening.
items: The first bright dot appears, often a planet
a: The first bright dot appears, often a planet
items.why: As the sky darkens after sunset, the brightest lights show first. Venus or Jupiter often appears before any star. The fainter stars appear when the sky is darker.

items.p: You walk past your window, and the paper strips slide past the Moon. Then you walk across the road to a far building and look again. Where is the Moon?
opts: Still in the same place in the sky
items.why: The Moon is so far that walking to the next building hardly changes where it is. That is why it seems to follow you everywhere.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: there is almost no air on the Moon. If you stood there, would the stars twinkle? Why?
items.a: No. Twinkling comes from moving air, and the Moon has almost no air, so the stars would shine steadily.
items.why: A strong answer says twinkling comes from moving air, and so a place with almost no air has no twinkling.

items.p: Draw the Sun, the Moon and you. Draw arrows to show how sunlight travels until you see the Moon.
items.a: An arrow from the Sun to the Moon, and an arrow from the Moon to the child's eyes.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the light starting at the Sun, landing on the Moon and bouncing to the child.
items.art: A blank space with a small Sun in one corner and a small child in the other.

items.p: Your friend says, 'The stars are tiny, as small as glitter.' Say out loud what you would tell her, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: The stars only look tiny because they are very far away. Each one is a sun, and some are much bigger than our Sun.
items.why: A strong answer says that the stars look small because they are far, and that they are really suns.

items.p: In the hot tawa test, the stove was switched off and the tawa cooled. What happened to the shivering?
items.why: As the tawa cooled, less warm air rose from it, so the light shivered less. Without moving warm air, the light looks steady.

items.p: Three of these usually twinkle. Which one usually does not? Circle it.
opts: A star low over the rooftops
A bright star such as Sirius
items.why: Venus is a planet and usually shines steadily. Stars twinkle because moving air shakes their light.

items.p: A grown-up reads each one. When you walk past a window, does it slide a lot, or hardly at all?
items: A paper strip on the window glass
A water tank on a far building
items.why: Near things slide past a lot when you move. Far things hardly slide, and the Moon is the farthest of all.

items.p: A friend says, 'Every bright dot in the night sky is a star.' Say out loud what you would tell her, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: Some bright dots are planets, and they shine steadily. Some are aeroplanes that move and blink red and green. Stars twinkle.
items.why: A strong answer names at least one other kind of bright dot and says how to tell it from a star.

items.p: Draw a line from each test to what it shows.
pairs: Near things slide past, and the far Moon stays put
Moving warm air makes a steady light shiver
Rolling a ball with your eyes shut
Beetles and people need to see the sky to go straight
items.why: Each test shows one idea from this unit: how far away the Moon is, why stars twinkle, and why a dung beetle watches the sky.

applications: Sailors and fishing families on the coasts of India have used the stars and the Moon to find their way and to know the tides.
Many Indian calendars count months by the Moon, so festivals like Diwali and Eid are set by its shape.
Astronomers use the 'near things slide more' rule, called parallax, to measure how far away stars are.
Pilots and sailors learn to tell planets, stars and aircraft lights apart at night.
Dark sky places such as Hanle in Ladakh keep lights low so that telescopes and people can see the stars.

spotted.text: On every full Moon night, thousands of people walk round the Arunachala hill at Tiruvannamalai, in Tamil Nadu, by moonlight.
spotted.art: Crowds walking along a road at night around a big hill, with a full Moon above.

spotted.text: Tamil children sing 'Nila nila odi vaa', asking the Moon to come running. In Kerala, the Moon is called Ambili Ammavan, Uncle Moon.
spotted.art: A mother on a balcony in Madurai holding a child on her hip and pointing at the full Moon.

spotted.text: Telugu families sing 'Chandamama raave' to little children, calling the Moon to come and play.
spotted.art: A grandmother feeding a small child rice from a steel plate under the Moon, on a terrace in Vijayawada.

spotted.text: On Kojagiri Purnima in Maharashtra, families stay up to see the full Moon and drink warm masala milk.
spotted.art: A family on a building terrace in Pune with steel tumblers of milk and a full Moon.

spotted.text: In Bengal, on the full Moon night after Durga Puja, families keep Kojagori Lakshmi Puja.
spotted.art: A Kolkata home with alpana patterns on the floor and a full Moon outside the window.

spotted.text: At the end of Ramzan, people all over India look for the thin new crescent Moon before Eid begins.
spotted.art: Families on a rooftop at dusk pointing at a very thin crescent Moon low in the west.

spotted.text: At Hanle in Ladakh, India's first Dark Sky Reserve, the sky is so dark that the Milky Way shines over the hills.
spotted.art: A telescope dome on a dry hill under a sky full of stars and a pale band of the Milky Way.

open_questions.why_open: Most scientists think a planet-sized rock crashed into the young Earth, and the Moon formed from the pieces. They still argue about how big the crash was and what the pieces were made of.

open_questions.q: Why does the Moon look so big when it is low near the rooftops?
open_questions.why_open: Photos show that the rising Moon is the same size as the Moon high up. It only looks bigger to us: the change is in how we see it, not in the Moon. Scientists still argue about exactly why.

open_questions.q: How do animals use the night sky?
open_questions.why_open: Dung beetles use the glow of the Milky Way, and some birds learn the stars to fly at night. Scientists are still finding out which animals use the sky, and what each one sees in it.

ask_kids: When we ride in the bus tonight, watch the Moon. Does it keep up with us?
Can you see the Moon in the daytime today? Let's look.
Which is the brightest dot in the sky tonight? Does it twinkle?
Which bright dot do you think is a planet? Why?
Who else might be looking at the same Moon right now?
If you stood on the Moon, what would you see in the sky?

jokes.j: Why did the Moon skip dinner?
Why did the star go to school?
What did the planet say to the twinkling star?
jokes.a: Calm down! Try shining steadily, like me.

jokes.j: What do stars do in the daytime?
jokes.a: They play hide and seek with the Sun!

jokes.j: Why did the aeroplane blink at the star?
jokes.a: It wanted to look like a star too!

jokes.j: What did the Sun say to the Moon?
jokes.a: Don't worry, I'll light you up!

jokes.j: Why did the cow go to space?
What kind of music do planets sing?
How do you throw a party in space?

maths.problem: You draw the Moon's face. You shade 3 big dark patches and 4 small ones. How many dark patches did you draw in all? Were there more big ones or small ones?
maths.answer: 7 patches. There were more small ones.
maths.explain: 3 big and 4 small make 7. 4 is more than 3, so there were more small patches.
maths.context: This is about the Look Closely at the Moon activity, where you drew the Moon's shape and its dark patches.
maths.why_maths: Counting and comparing the patches helps us check our drawing against the real Moon next time.

maths.problem: You stick 3 paper strips on the window. Then you stick 3 more. How many strips are on the window now?
maths.explain: 3 strips and 3 more strips make 6 strips.
maths.context: This is about the window strip test, where you walked past a window and watched the Moon.
maths.why_maths: Counting the strips helps us set up the window strip test and check what we see.

maths.problem: You watch 6 bright dots in the evening sky. 4 of them twinkle. The rest shine steadily. How many shine steadily? What might they be?
maths.answer: 2 shone steadily. They might be planets.
maths.explain: 6 dots, and 4 of them twinkled. 6 take away 4 is 2. So 2 dots shone steadily. Planets usually shine steadily, so they might be planets.
maths.context: This is about the twinkle or steady activity, where you watched bright dots in the evening sky.
maths.why_maths: Counting the steady dots shows how many might be planets, so we know how many to look for again next week.

maths.problem: Look at the sky picture. Venus is to the left of the Moon. A star is above the Moon. An aeroplane is to the right of the Moon. What is between Venus and the aeroplane?
maths.explain: Venus is on the left of the Moon, and the aeroplane is on the right. So the Moon is in the middle, between them.
maths.context: This is about finding things in the night sky by saying where they are.
maths.why_maths: Words like left, right and above help us tell someone exactly where to look in the sky.
maths.art: A night sky with a bright dot labelled Venus on the left, the Moon in the middle, a star above the Moon and a blinking aeroplane on the right.

founder: Curriculum entry sci.sky.stargazing.L1 (looking at the night sky: Moon, bright stars, planets), and the founder's notebook item phy:41 (observational astronomy: naked-eye sky, constellations, planets). No board chapter is listed for this level.
ideas/by_topic/the-universe-sun-moon-stars-and-planets.md: the notebook's women astronomers (SCI cards) shaped the choice to credit Marie Dacke. Its galaxy and expansion grids belong to later levels.

The Level 3 stargazing unit teaches constellations, nakshatras, dark-adapted eyes and the Moon's daily step among the stars. This unit leaves all of those to it, and prepares for them with naming what is in the sky, twinkling, and why the Moon seems to follow us.

The sister unit sci.sky.sun-moon-stars.L1 already has the torch-in-the-sun test, the window star count and the city lights card, so this unit does not repeat them. It covers why the Moon seems to follow us, twinkling, star colours and telling planets and aeroplanes from stars.
science: Average Earth to Moon distance: about 384,400 km. At 80 km per hour without stopping, that is about 4,800 hours, or about 200 days.

M. Dacke, E. Baird, M. Byrne, C. H. Scholtz and E. J. Warrant, 'Dung beetles use the Milky Way for orientation', Current Biology 23 (2013): beetles rolled straight under a starry sky and a planetarium Milky Way, and lost their way when the sky was hidden.

Aristotle, On the Heavens, Book 2, chapter 8: the planets do not twinkle because they are near, and the stars twinkle because our sight trembles over the great distance. Isaac Newton, Opticks (1704), Book 1: twinkling comes from the trembling of the air, and telescopes work best in the still air of high mountains.
Chandrayaan-3's Vikram lander touched down near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023.
Hanle, Ladakh, was declared India's first Dark Sky Reserve in 2022.
Brahmabindu Upanishad 12 (eka eva hi bhutatma ... jalacandravat). Su Shi, 'Shui Diao Ge Tou' (Mid-Autumn, 1076).

roots.context: In the window strip test, you walked past a window. The paper strips slid by, and the Moon stayed in the same place. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the window strip test, the paper strips slid past when you walked, but the Moon stayed put. Near things change place when you move. The Moon is so far that a few steps hardly change where you see it. So the Moon seems to follow everyone who looks at it, all at once.
deep_truth.habit: We feel that a thing which keeps up with us must be near us, or following us. The window strip test shows the opposite: the Moon keeps up because it is so very far away.
deep_truth.evidence: In the window strip test, the near strips slid past fast, a far building slid a little, and the Moon did not move at all. In the One Moon, Two Windows project, someone in another town draws the same Moon at the same time.

three.who_am_i: You are one of millions of people looking up at the same Moon tonight. Where you stand changes what is near you, but not the Moon.
three.what_is_life: Many living beings use the night sky. A dung beetle rolls straight by the Milky Way, birds fly by the stars at night, and you find the Moon from your window.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is much bigger than it looks. The Moon seems to sit just above the rooftops, but it is much farther than any building or hill.

roots.thread: There is one Moon. Tonight it shines in the window of every home that faces it, from Kochi to Kohima. Each child sees it from their own place, and each thinks it came along with them. Everything is aware in its own way, the Moon too. Many scientists disagree: they say only living beings with nerves are aware.

teachings.teaching: There is one Self in all beings. It is seen as one and as many, like the one Moon reflected in many pots of water.
teachings.link: The Upanishad uses the one Moon seen in many places as a picture of one Self in many beings. The window strip test showed why one Moon can be seen from so many places at once: it is very far away. The teaching is a picture, not a proof.

teachings.source: Su Shi, 'Shui Diao Ge Tou' (China, Mid-Autumn night, 1076)
teachings.teaching: The poet Su Shi missed his brother, who lived far away. He wished that they could both live long, and share the beauty of the same Moon, though a thousand miles apart.
teachings.link: Su Shi knew that two people far apart see the same Moon at the same time, as you do when you phone someone in another town.

science.text: Near things seem to shift more than far things when you move. Astronomers call this parallax, and they use it to measure how far away the nearer stars are.
The Moon is about 3,84,000 kilometres away. Its light reaches us in just over one second.

other_view.who: Scientists who study how we see
other_view.view: They say each person's eyes and brain build their own picture of the Moon. So in one way there are as many Moons as there are people looking, even though there is one Moon in the sky.

practice.title: One Moon, many windows
practice.say: Stand at the window and find the Moon. If it is not up, look at the brightest star. Breathe in slowly, and breathe out slowly, five times. Now think of someone far away. They might be looking at the same Moon right now. Send them a kind thought.
practice.kid: Find the Moon. Breathe in and out slowly, five times. Think of someone far away. They may see this Moon too.

ask: The Moon seemed to come along with you, and with someone far away, at the same time. Whose Moon is it?
The Moon's light started at the Sun. When you see the Moon, are you also seeing the Sun?
If nobody in the whole world looked at the Moon tonight, would it still be shining?
roots.art: Many windows of different homes across India, from a Kerala house to a hill town flat, each with a child looking up at the same Moon in one sky.

how_we_found_out.story: About 2,300 years ago, the Greek thinker Aristotle noticed something about the night sky. The stars twinkle, but the planets mostly shine steadily. He thought he knew why. The planets are nearer, he said. The stars are very far, so our sight gets tired and trembles on the long way to them, and that makes them seem to twinkle. He was right that the planets are much nearer than the stars. But the trembling is not in our sight. In 1704, the English scientist Isaac Newton wrote that twinkling comes from the air. The air above us is always moving, and it shakes the light passing through it. He said telescopes would work best on the tops of high mountains, where the air is calm. Today India has a telescope at Hanle in Ladakh, about 4,500 metres up. And telescopes sent into space, above all the air, see stars that do not twinkle at all.
how_we_found_out.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker; Isaac Newton, an English scientist
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Aristotle thought stars twinkle because our sight trembles on its long trip to them. Newton wrote that the trembling is in the moving air, and telescopes in space, above the air, see stars shine without twinkling.

playtest: Walked through every card, game and experiment as a parent and a six-year-old in a flat. Shortened the four explanation cards to 3-4 sentences. The tawa test now stands the phone on a steel box, not paper books near the flame. The sorting game's last step now matches its check, and a tie is a shared win. The moving game no longer says the Moon player's arms 'point'. The dung beetle is no longer 'she'. The scooter challenge no longer asks a rider to watch the Moon while riding. The core sheet's repeated odd-one-out became a drawing of the moving strip, and a repeated 'why the bus Moon' question became a train question. The stretch sheet's steps now print out of order, and its repeated light question became 'would stars twinkle on the Moon?'. One joke was replaced and a repeated distance line was removed.
